newsitem.title: USA: Oozing package at U.S. Jewish group sparks alert.
newsitem.headline: Oozing package at U.S. Jewish group sparks alert.

text.p: An oozing package containing a menacing note was sent to a Jewish organisation on Thursday, sparking a major security alert, but the FBI later determined that the substance was "not life-threatening."

The downtown building housing B'nai B'rith, and surrounding streets, were sealed off for hours as officials dealt with the suspicious package that leaked a pungent red liquid police originally identified as "biological material."
Military disposal experts gingerly removed the package, which had been mailed to the Jewish gropu, and took it to the U.S. Naval Medical Research Institute in nearby Bethesda, Maryland, for testing.

"The substance is not life-threatening as claimed in the letter that accompanies the package," FBI official Thomas Pickard said late on Thursday. "Testing will continue to positively identify the substance."
Pickard said all necessary precautions had been taken to contain the incident until scientific testing conclusively determined it was not an actual biological agent.
"These incidents require extreme caution and substantial expertise to determine if the threat is real," he added.

The office in bustling downtown Washington, D.C., about six blocks from the White House, was sealed off and 108 people in the building kept inside as a precaution until scientists determined the nature of the substance.
"We found some biological material and a note that was left with the package," District of Columbia Police Chief Larry Soulsby said.
"An 8x10 envelope was found in our mailroom with red liquid coming out of it" late on Thursday morning, B'nai B'rith spokeswoman Robin Schwartz-Kreger told Reuters by telephone.
She said it was accompanied by a "threatening" letter but she did not know the nature of the threats.
Hazardous material experts in bright blue and white protective suits and gas-masks removed the package from outside the building housing B'nai B'rith's international headquarters.
Nearby George Washington University Hospital reported that 15 to 18 people had been sent in for observation as a precaution.

Police said 14 people, 12 law enforcement and fire officials and two civilians, were decontaminated at the scene also as a precaution. One person was seen outside the building strapped in a medical chair being sprayed with a decontaminant by a white-clad rescue team.

Although the U.S. capital suffers false-alarm security scares fairly routinely because of its concentration of federal agencies and interest groups, this one mobilised local police and fire units, FBI agents and military hazardous material experts.
